results.summary: This project is an essentially undocumented placeholder with the title custom_lol, a one-line description of sdfdf, and a how-it-works section reading only Hallloooooo halloooooo. The pin names are generic numbered inputs and outputs, with the only stated external hardware being an LED, and the testing note is just hallooo. There is not enough information to determine any logic function, interface, or intended application. The design is best treated as a workshop or template experiment with no meaningful behaviour documented.

The project is titled gatekeeping the gates and is described as a got your gates, with eight inputs named input a through input h and eight outputs named out 0 through out 7. The documentation states only that it is something being done during a workshop and gives no description of the actual gate arrangement or logic equations. The testing section is a joke line from Portal rather than a procedure, and the external-hardware field was left as the template text. As a result, the design cannot be pinned down beyond being a Wokwi workshop exercise in gate-level logic.

This project is titled RTX 8090 and has the one-line description descripstion tbd, with only two pins both named tbd. The documentation consists of Hello i am making a chip lol followed by template instructions, a test line of yessir, and an external-hardware field reading hello. No function, interface, or test procedure is actually specified. The submission is a placeholder created during a workshop or template pass and contains no usable design information.

This design is a quick clock-divider test in which the input clock is routed to output 7 and a divide-by-four version is routed to output 0. An enable input on ui[0] gates the divider, and the documented test procedure is to hold the enable low and wait four seconds, then raise it and press reset for one second. It runs at a 1 Hz clock in Wokwi and needs no external hardware. It is a minimal verification exercise rather than a complete application.

Titled TinyTapeout logic gate test and described only as Test, this block maps ui[1] through ui[5] to the values 2 through 6 and drives uo[0] and uo[1] to the values 1 and 2. The documentation says only that it is for testing and that the user should press a button, with no explanation of the underlying logic. No external hardware is listed, and it is unclear whether the block performs any meaningful computation. The project is best understood as a test or factory-test submission rather than a designed function.

This block is titled Test and described as just a test, and it drives a 7-segment display with an upper bar on uo[0] and a dot on uo[7]. One enable input controls clocked pins while a second enable makes the dot permanent, so the upper bar blinks when clocked and the dot can be latched on. The documented test is to activate pins 1 and 2, and the only external hardware required is a 7-segment display. It is a small display-driver demonstration rather than a full application.

Titled My Tiny Tapeout and described as Test123, this project has a single input pin on ui[0] labelled input 1 and no outputs listed. The documentation repeats Test 1234 and Test 134 without explaining what the design computes, and the external-hardware field also contains only Test 12343. There is no description of a function, interface, or test procedure. It appears to be a completely empty placeholder created during template setup.

The project is titled Custom_ASIC and its one-line description states that it is preliminary and not yet working. The pin list is a set of bare numbered inputs and outputs, and the how-it-works and testing sections both repeat that it is currently just a test of random design. No external hardware is specified and no actual circuit function is documented. It should be regarded as an early-stage placeholder rather than a working design.

This block is titled 83rk: Tiny Tapeout and implements an SR flip-flop using inputs a and b and presenting AND, NAND and OR outputs along with divided clocks on outputs 3 and 4. The documented test is simply to set and reset the flip-flop while checking the output values, and no external hardware is required. It runs in Wokwi with a 10000 Hz clock and the design is a simple combinational and sequential logic demonstration rather than a complete application. The documentation is very brief but consistent with the pin names.

Titled Test and described as Test, this project has inputs in 1 through in 6 and a single output, with documentation simply saying it works because it works. The test procedure is push start and the external-hardware field contains the word dunno. No logic function, interface, or circuit behaviour is actually described. It is another essentially empty placeholder submission.
